title: Recognising a binary search tree
focus: Name the parts of a tree and explain the BST rule.
intro: A registrar can find a name in a sorted class list by comparing entries. A binary search tree (BST) uses the same idea, but records are connected in branches.

sections.heading: The parts of a tree
sections.body: A tree is made of nodes joined by links. A binary tree gives each node at most two children: one left child and one right child.
items: The top node, which has no parent.
Nodes directly connected by one link.
A node and every node below it through its links.

sections.heading: The BST rule applies to whole subtrees
sections.body: At every node, every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger. Checking only a node against its direct children is not enough.
sections.caption: This binary tree is not a BST: 60 is in 50's left subtree even though 60 is greater than 50.

sections.heading: Remember
sections.body: A chain can still be a valid BST; the rule does not require the tree to be balanced. A missing child is an empty subtree.

title: Searching and inserting
focus: Trace searches, insertions, and a list of values in its given order.
intro: The registrar needs to find and add student records. Start at the root and compare the target with one node at a time.

sections.heading: Search for 60
sections.body: If the target matches the current key, stop. If it is smaller, follow the left link; if larger, follow the right link. Repeat at the next node.
sections.caption: The search path is 50 -> 70 -> 60. Search follows one path rather than checking every node.

sections.heading: An unsuccessful search can find an insertion position
sections.body: Searching for 65 follows 50 -> 70 -> 60 -> EMPTY. To insert 65, attach it at that empty right-child link of 60. Existing nodes stay where they are.
sections.caption: 65 is placed as the right child of 60, after following the same comparisons as a search.

sections.heading: Build in the order given
sections.body: Start with an empty tree and insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 in exactly that order. Do not sort the input first; changing the order can change the tree's shape.

title: Depth-first traversals
focus: Trace pre-order, in-order, and post-order and explain sorted output.
intro: A traversal visits every node. The traversal rule determines when a node's key is written to the output.

sections.heading: Three visit orders
sections.body: Finish a subtree before moving to the next one. An empty subtree contributes no output.

sections.heading: Trace the reference tree
sections.body: For this tree, pre-order writes the root first; in-order writes the left subtree first; post-order writes the root last.

sections.heading: Why in-order is sorted
sections.body: In a BST, every left-subtree key is smaller than the node and every right-subtree key is larger. In-order visits left, node, then right, so the resulting keys are ascending. On a tree that is not a BST, in-order is not necessarily sorted.

title: Complexity and choosing a structure
focus: Explain how insertion order affects search cost and compare a BST with a sorted array.
intro: An ordinary BST does not rebalance itself. The order in which records arrive can make the tree shallow or chain-shaped.

sections.heading: Insertion order changes shape
sections.body: Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order makes each new value the right child of the previous one. Inserting 3, 2, 4, 1, 5 gives a shorter tree.

sections.heading: Search cost follows height
sections.body: A search examines at most height + 1 stored nodes. A roughly balanced BST can search in O(log n); a chain can need O(n) comparisons. An ordinary BST does not guarantee balance.

sections.heading: BST or sorted array?
sections.body: A BST can attach a new key without shifting later records, but its shape may deteriorate. A sorted array supports O(log n) binary search, but inserting into the middle can require O(n) shifts.
items: A sorted array is a good fit: binary search is logarithmic and there are few inserts.
A BST may avoid shifting records, but search and insert can be linear if arrival order creates a chain.
